Dermatology · published research

Wart ablation site healing

Two uncontrolled reports describe healing by about day 15 after plantar-wart ablation followed by red LED, but do not isolate the LED contribution. A separate case of digital ischemia after wart surgery improved during combined care.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two uncontrolled reports describe healing by about day 15 after plantar-wart ablation followed by red LED, but do not isolate the LED contribution. A separate case of digital ischemia after wart surgery improved during combined care.

Summary of the Evidence

Three publications are relevant to healing after wart removal. Two uncontrolled reports from the same Spanish centre describe plantar warts treated by Er:YAG ablation followed by red LED. Their patient and lesion counts differ, and overlap is possible, so they should not be added as separate independent cohorts. A third case report concerns severe digital ischemia after a complicated laser procedure for a subungual wart. It is a narrow related observation, not a study of routine plantar-wart healing. No controlled trial or animal or cell study directly tests this indication.

Human and clinical evidence

The 2005 report described 141 plantar-wart cases in 133 patients. The wounds reportedly shrank by day 6 and had usually closed by day 15; 11 cases recurred by 12 months. A 2006 report described 121 warts in 58 patients, with usual closure by day 15 and recurrence in 3 of 58 patients. Both reports combined wart removal, LED exposure, and postoperative care and had no comparator that omitted LED. The recurrence figures therefore describe outcomes after the treatment package, not an LED effect on viral clearance (Trelles & Calderhead 2005 Trelles et al. 2006).

In a separate case, a patient developed digital ischemia and gangrene after CO₂-laser treatment and tourniquet use for a subungual wart. Skin color and function improved during treatment that included red PBM, dressings, and medication. Because these measures were given together and there was no control, the case cannot determine how much recovery came from PBM (Source).

Animal evidence

No animal study of post-ablation wart wounds was identified in the relevant records.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell-culture or ex-vivo study directly addressing post-ablation wart healing was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The plantar-wart reports used 633-nm red visible LED for 20 minutes around the wound. The 2005 report gave 126 J/cm² per session and repeated treatment immediately and on postoperative days 2, 3, 6, and 10; the 2006 report used 96 J/cm² and repeated treatment on days 2, 6, and 10. Er:YAG ablation settings also differed between reports. The ischemia case used 633-nm red light at 126 J/cm² for 20 minutes, three times weekly for five weeks. These distinct regimens were not compared directly.

Interpretation

The published cases describe prompt closure and low recurrence after combined wart ablation and LED care. Those outcomes are favorable observations, but the studies cannot show how much the LED changed healing beyond ablation and routine care. They also do not establish that PBM prevents wart recurrence.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for a PBM-specific healing effect after wart ablation
Publications and records3 relevant articles (two reports likely overlap)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two uncontrolled reports describe wounds usually closing by about day 15 after Er:YAG wart ablation followed by red LED, but the LED was always combined with ablation and routine care. The reports may include overlapping patients. A controlled comparison that keeps ablation and wound care identical, then measures closure, pain, infection, and recurrence, would show whether LED adds benefit.
